#4721. Obesity in Your 20s and 30s May Increase Cancer Risk Later in Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Younger adults with obesity may be more likely to develop cancer before midlife than those who maintain a moderate weight, according to a study published on October 26 in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

The risk for cancer became higher as weight increased. The highest rates were seen in those with severe obesity and abdominal obesity.

This highlights the potential importance of weight management in the prevention of early onset cancer.

Rates of both obesity and early onset cancer are rising among younger adults globally.

This study analyzed data from the Korean National Health Insurance Service database. The researchers identified 6,313,338 adults ages 20 to 39 who had no history of cancer and who underwent standardized national health screenings.

The researchers followed the participants for an average of 11 years.

Body mass index (BMI) was categorized into five groups ranging from underweight to class II obesity using the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria for Asian populations. Waist circumference was also measured as an indicator of abdominal adiposity.

During the analysis, the researchers adjusted for various factors such as:

Over the follow-up period, there were 151,893 cases of cancer among the participants. The incidence rate increased progressively based on obesity categories, from 1.84% in “normal-weight” individuals to 2.24% in class I obesity and 2.62% in class II obesity.

The strongest associations were seen in the following cancers:

Obesity was not associated with breast cancer diagnosed before the age of 50.

Ketan Thanki, MD, board certified colorectal surgeon with the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in Long Beach, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, explained to Healthline that obesity itself causes states that promote cancer formation.

This current study focused on the Korean population. However, the connection between obesity and cancer risk is a global issue.

Previous research has shown that around 10% of all new cancer diagnoses in the United States are associated with obesity. Obesity also accounts for up to 50% of certain cancers, including endometrial and liver cancer.

The study also showed that waist circumference, which indicates abdominal obesity, may be linked to cancer risk that is similar to that of individuals with overweight.

The study researchers used the thresholds set out by the Korean Society for the Study of Obesity. These thresholds put the waist circumference cutoff at over 90 cm (35.4 in) for males and over 85cm (33.46 in) for females.

These are not universal cutoffs. According to the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), waist circumference measurements that can increase your risk of negative health issues are 101.6 cm (40 in) for males and 88.9 cm (35 in) for females.

Previous research has also suggested an association between waist circumference and cancer risk, independent of BMI. One study showed a potential 11% increased risk of cancer in people with a waist circumference over the thresholds, even if they were physically active.

The current study found that males had a higher relative association between obesity and cancer, while females showed higher absolute risk.

The researchers also found that the absolute risk was higher in adults ages 30 to 39.

Those who currently smoke or who have ever smoked were also found to have a higher risk of developing cancer than those who have never smoked.

“Diet, exercise, and now medications can all be used very effectively to reduce one’s weight and, hopefully as a result, cancer risk,” Thanki said.

He also noted that, due to differences between South Korean populations and those in other countries such as the United States, further studies will be needed to determine how this translates across other populations.

“But I think this trend will likely extend across all cultures,” he said.

#4720. Do you need a preventative rabies vaccine? Probably not.

Published Nov 3, 2026 8:07 AM EST

Of all the deadly diseases that can spread from mammals to humans, rabies is the most infamous. Cujo had it. Old Yeller had it. A squirrel in “National Lampoon’s Christmas Vacation” had it. Unfortunately, this virus doesn’t only live in fiction. It kills at least 59,000 people a year and is present in over 150 countries. On that list is the U.S., which is seeing a nationwide surge in reported cases of human exposures to rabid or possibly rabid animals.

If left untreated, rabies is always fatal (both for animals and humans). On the bright side, it’s also 100 percent preventable. Typically, in the U.S., humans get vaccinated for rabies after suspected rabies exposure, but right now many of us are wondering: Can and should you get vaccinated against rabies just as a precaution? Is there any benefit in getting a preventative rabies vaccine? The simple answer is no. Getting a pre-exposure vaccine doesn’t protect you from contracting the disease, and if you have an encounter with an animal that might have rabies, you’ll still need to get follow up doses regardless.

Before diving in, let’s clear up some common misconceptions about rabies and the rabies vaccine. Rabies is a zoonotic virus that comes in two types: furious rabies and paralytic rabies. Both types of rabies attack the central nervous system and both are fatal. Any mammal can be infected with rabies, and if infected, can transmit it to other animals or humans through a bite or scratch—even if you can’t see or feel the wound. Though rabies doesn’t turn its victims into people-eating zombies, as Hollywood would have us believe, it does deliver an acutely agonizing death.

The modern vaccine for rabies is made from cell culture. A cell culture vaccine contains no live virus. It is literally impossible for you to get rabies from the vaccine, which, you may be surprised to hear, is also pretty painless.

“The rabies vaccine is no more painful than a flu shot,” Dr. Edward R. Rensimer, a board-certified doctor of infectious diseases and internal medicine and director of the International Medicine Center in Houston, tells Popular Science.

If exposed to a rabid or possibly rabid animal, you will require more than one dose of a rabies vaccine.

“The injection site and number of doses recommended are dependent on the type of exposure you’ve had to a potentially rabid animal,” says Dr. Mirava Yuson, an epidemiologist and postdoctoral researcher working at the UCLA TIDE (Translational Infectious Disease Eco-epidemiology) Lab.

“You can expect, for example, that a bite wound induced by an animal that’s suspected to be rabid, versus a light scratch from an animal that is not suspected to have rabies, will merit different doses and numbers of recommended boosters that are needed to complete a vaccine series.”

Both Yuson and Rensimer cannot overstate the safety and efficacy of the rabies vaccine and emphasize that side effects, should they occur, are minimal.

“It is analogous to the flu vaccine,” Rensimer says, adding that in his more than 45 years of administering the vaccine he’s never seen a major adverse event.

“A very small minority of people in the 24 hours after the first dose may have low-grade fever, body aches, and malaise.”

So, the rabies vaccine is a totally safe, 100 percent effective, and generally gentle vaccine? Sign us up! In all seriousness, why wouldn’t we get this vaccine, regardless of exposure risk, especially now, when rabies outbreaks and mass rabies exposure events are on the rise across the U.S.? Turns out there are a couple reasons why getting the rabies vaccine without any known risk exposure doesn’t make sense.

First, the “better safe than sorry” approach doesn’t work with rabies. Getting a rabies shot before a risk exposure event does not prevent you from becoming infected with rabies, nor does it minimize the effects of the fatal virus should you get it. You will still die if untreated by vaccinations post-exposure.

“There is a pre-exposure rabies vaccine that people get before traveling to rabies-endemic areas; however, the problem is, even if you get it, the minute you are exposed to a potentially rabid animal, you need a second dose, the post-exposure vaccine,” Yuson says.

“Veterinary professionals like me get them every year, but that does not preclude us from needing a post-exposure dose should we be potentially exposed. One vaccine is never enough and that is supremely important to know.”

Inside the school where dogs learn to sniff out bed bugs and other pests

Why do dogs’ legs shake during pets? It’s not because they like it.

Could a whale really swallow a human? We asked a biologist.

Second, getting a rabies vaccine regardless of risk exposure could confuse your case for clinicians if you do eventually face potential risk exposure.

“Getting the vaccine without known risk exposure can unfortunately cause some issues with the next dose should you be exposed or possibly exposed to a rabid animal,” Yuson says. “It becomes a question [for doctors]: ‘Do we start the regimen all over?’”

The best way to stay safe is also a bit of a bummer: It’s to limit contact with wildlife. All mammals are capable of getting infected with and transmitting rabies. In the U.S., there are infected raccoons, foxes, skunks and, most of all, bats, which are responsible for 70 percent of rabies deaths in people.

“The thing with bats, without getting too technical, is that they’re the only flying mammals,” Yuson says. “They can transmit diseases over great distances and can carry multiple diseases without themselves being sick, and they have very small fangs. You may not even feel the bite or often won’t see a bite wound.”

Because you may not even know you were bitten, it’s imperative that, after any encounter with a bat or any other potentially rabid creature, you immediately go to the ER and get the first of what will likely be a few post-exposure vaccines.

The vaccine is literally the only way to survive if you’ve been infected. There is no “wait and see” window, either.

“Once symptoms manifest, there is no cure for rabies; it has a 100 percent mortality rate and the only way to prevent infection after exposure is through vaccination,” Yuson says.

It’s a scary time, and rabies is a very scary virus, but remember that even with the spike in reported cases of human exposures to rabid or possibly rabid animals, a human dying from rabies is, in the U.S. at least, an incredibly rare thing.

“We average one to six cases of rabies a year in the U.S.,” Rensimer says.

Unfortunately, because of rising temperatures (rabies loves warm weather) and continued encroachment on wildlife habitats by good old mankind (leads to increased exposure risk among humans and pets), rabies doesn’t look to be going anywhere anytime soon.

But thanks to science, there’s no real reason to worry, because if for any reason we do come into contact with a possibly rabid animal, there’s a safe, accessible, and 100 percent effective vaccine available.

#4719. Can a Sleep Divorce Save Your Marriage?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 11, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

Part of being a family lawyer is knowing how to divorce a couple. Meaning, how to extricate two people from a legal union so they can stand on their own two feet as they move forward independently and, if applicable, as co-parents afterward. This is the obvious part of what I do. The other, less obvious role I have is figuring out whether someone who ends up on a call with me actually needs me for a dissolution.

I suspect I’m dealing with the latter situation when someone tells me they aren’t sleeping, they’re up all night because their partner’s waking or keeping them up, and that it’s negatively affecting their marriage in every way imaginable: they’re irritable, resentful, experiencing weight gain, and a slew of other health problems. They’re also too tired to have sex, so they’ve stopped or practically stopped. But, and this is key, they also tell me they love their spouse and the life they’ve built together and aren’t sure if they want to take such a hard approach, at least just yet.

I’m not a medical doctor, but I’ve been married twice, this time to my forever partner, so I recognize how important sleep is for quality of life and how different sleep habits can cause a host of issues if you don’t keep them in check. This is why I suggest getting to the bottom of what’s keeping you awake at night and, if need be, engaging in what’s colloquially known as a sleep divorce, where you and your partner stay married and do everything married couples typically do—except sleep in the same bed. But before going this route, here’s what I suggest doing first.

According to a 2017 study, more than one-third of Americans don’t get enough sleep, and it’s taking a toll not only on people’s physical health but on their mental health as well. The researchers leading the study suggest that those who are sleep-deprived find it more challenging to be positive-minded than those who are adequately rested, and that an inability to be positive is a common symptom of depression. Depression, another study finds, can increase the likelihood of divorce. Based on these conclusions, it might be worth considering whether your thoughts about the quality of your marriage are actually rooted in the quality of your sleep or something else.

The most obvious way to find out whether poor sleep is the culprit in your marital woes is to actually start getting a good night’s sleep. If you’re keeping your partner up at night, or your partner is keeping you awake because of an apparent medical issue, such as snoring, it’s time to visit a specialist for a sleep study. A sleep study provides data so a medical practitioner can understand what’s going on physically during the night and address it.

If your health is being negatively affected by a partner disrupting your sleep, what’s causing them to wake you may pose a similar or even greater health risk for them. If you aren’t sleeping because your partner is simply inconsiderate, it’s time to address that as well with a conversation and some ground rules.

Trial and error should become your M.O. If you’re first attempting to get to the bottom of a medical mystery, it may take weeks to months to get the answers you need and, once you do, to treat the issue. In the meantime, you may want to try a few other approaches.

That may include adjusting the bedroom temperature and reducing any light coming in. It may also include the person without the medical issue heading to bed first so it’s easier for them to fall asleep, getting earplugs, or moving to a different location once they’ve been woken up. If all else fails, it may be time to try sleeping in separate rooms, aka, get a sleep divorce.

A lot can happen in the bedroom in the moments before falling asleep, and if you’re retreating to separate rooms at this time, you may want to do the following so you and your spouse don’t become further disconnected, causing a sleep divorce to become a precursor to a real divorce.

Spending time together before bed, engaging in personal touch that’s not intended to lead to sex, is an important practice to maintain. Hold hands while watching TV, lay your head on your partner’s shoulder, cuddle under a blanket. If you’re comfortable visiting each other’s bedrooms and doing these things there until it’s time to actually go to sleep, try that. Communicate about what’s comfortable for both of you, then make it a habit.

If you’re finding that due to sleeping in separate bedrooms, sex isn’t happening organically, schedule it or make a point to suggest it. Given you’re not in the same bed where sex may be easier to initiate, you may have to rely on using your words more than in the past. Sleeping together less shouldn’t equate to communicating less. Even better is if it leads to communicating more. Speaking of which…

Whether you’re planning on having sex or not, or are basking in the afterglow, lying together in bed before falling asleep is when couples have their most intimate conversations. A sleep divorce can interfere with that if you let it. So don’t.

Not only should you make time for these conversations, but you should savor them. The more quality conversations you engage in, the closer you become. In my experience, spouses who invest time and attention into each other and their marriages tend to stay married. Where you sleep is far less consequential than what you do when you’re awake.

#4718. Arrow the fearless black bear doesn’t care if a foe is bigger

Published Nov 3, 2026 10:31 AM EST

If you are of a certain age, you might remember an innocent time when the honey badger (Mellivora capensis) took over the internet. Viral videos showing the feisty mammals that “don’t care” and punching above their weight made the honey badger a poster species for fearlessness.

That same spirit appears to be alive and well in a bear named Arrow. The U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest has awarded the black bear (Ursus americanus) with the 2026 Honey Badger Award.

Arrow is designated by a scar on his ear, and a thin white bit of fur by his nose that resembles a mustache. According to the rangers, Arrow has also always been a fearless bear. He suffered an injury to his back left leg during a fight with a black bear named Tatonka in 2019. He still walks with a limp, but that has not dampened his resolve.

“This year, Arrow challenged and backed down two different brown bears,” the rangers write. “Usually, brown bears are dominant over black bears due to the significant size disparity. But there are so many fish to be had at Anan Creek, the bigger bears frequently choose avoidance over violence.”

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of Southeast Alaska, including the capital city of Juneau. The large area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Like their chunky counterparts further north in Katmai National Park, the bears return annually each summer to eat salmon and teach their cubs how to fish and survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here exhibits their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted here, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics and behaviors.

#4716. Letter From the Editor-in-Chief: What a Decade of Bedtime Stories Taught Me About Health

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

I’ve read to my children each night at bedtime for as long as I (and they) can remember. We started with the likes of “Goodnight Batcave” and the lesser-known-in-the-US but oh-so-wonderful collection of verse-driven classics from former UK Children’s Laureate Julia Donaldson.

We moved on to B.J. Novak’s anarchic love letter to the power of words (and to great typography), “The Book With No Pictures.”

We eventually worked our way up to Roald Dahl’s wickedly dark back catalog, discovering more complex characters, language and plotting as we went.

When my eldest, Amelia, hit 6, it was time to roll out the big guns.

Over the last 5 years (she’s now 11), I’ve read the seven Harry Potter books aloud twice, complete with all the voices: once to Amelia on her own, once to both her and her brother, Henry, two years her junior.

I had feared she wouldn’t be keen on another helping, but Amelia immersed herself once more in the world of Hogwarts with no hesitation and took immense joy in watching Henry discover for himself every twist and turn on Harry’s journey.

We have done the same thing with Tolkien’s “The Hobbit” and his fantasy masterpiece “The Lord of the Rings,” and are currently midway through “The Two Towers” on our second go around.

There’s a huge amount of reciprocal joy we take from this nightly ritual, beyond the practical benefits of providing a calming demarcation between the end of the day and the wind-down to sleep.

For me, it comes as either a break in my working day or a signal that it’s over, depending on how hectic things are.

For the kids, it’s an all-too-rare chance to get me all to themselves, no deadlines, screens, or other distractions to pull me away from being anything but 100% present.

For all three of us, it’s a literal (and literary!) warm blanket — a chance to escape under the covers to familiar worlds and familiar faces. It is, in short, incredibly good for our well-being.

And yet, in the world of health information — including on this site — thousands, if not millions, of reading hours are dedicated to the benefits of nutrition, sleep, and exercise as the building blocks of good health. Reading itself rarely makes that shortlist.

For me, it unequivocally deserves a place on it. Research seems to support that case. Even if we need more of it to really understand how and why.

A recent editorial in Psychological Medicine co-authored by Barbara Sahakian, Professor of Clinical Neuropsychology at Cambridge University, draws on a broad range of research linking reading for pleasure to better mental health and greater empathy.

The positive impact of reading on young people — just like Amelia and Henry — lso carries evidence.

Among more than 10,000 US adolescents, those who started reading for pleasure early had fewer mental health problems, spent less time on screens and slept more. Although, per an earlier column of mine, I can’t vouch for the sleep side of things when it comes to early bird Henry.

For many, reading can be a form of therapy that improves well-being. Bibliotherapy is a complementary therapeutic tool for emotional release and reduced stress and anxiety, with its roots traced back to ancient civilizations.

There’s even research suggesting a link between a love of reading and a lower risk of cognitive decline.

In a 2003 study of people aged 75 and over, reading was associated with a 35% lower risk of dementia over roughly five years.

A separate 14-year study from 2022 found that people who read at least weekly saw less cognitive decline, whatever their level of education.

A happy (and healthy) by-product of this love of being read to is that both my kids have now started reading to me at bedtime. Henry recently read “Jeffy the Burglar’s Cat” to us, a lesser-known but no less compelling chapter book by Ursula Moray Williams that was a staple of my own childhood. And we’ve enjoyed several books from Amelia, including the wistful tale of friendship and the circle of life, “Charlotte’s Web” by E.B. White – not a dry eye in the house for the final few chapters of that one.

They’ve also gone off and re-read the Harry Potter books and “The Hobbit” to themselves.

The research above links reading to many health benefits: better attention and memory, fewer mental health problems, more sleep, less time on screens, and greater empathy. I haven’t measured any of those impacts empirically in our house. Nor am I naive to the fact that as they get older, they’ll ultimately grow out of me reading to them, with school, extracurricular activities, their friends, and inevitably screens competing for more and more of their time.

Come what may, though, I know that a child who considers missing a reading session as the most cardinal of cardinal sins, and who scrambles for the chance to read aloud to their dad at bedtime is, at that moment, concentrating, empathizing, discovering and growing.

Researchers are clear that studies espousing the benefits of reading show association rather than proof, and it’s evident that more experimental work and deeper research are needed to ensure the complex cause and effect stands on firm scientific ground.

Regardless, it’s a healthy habit Amelia, Henry and I are very happy to keep, and with a bit of luck, I’ll get to pass it on to their kids one day.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

#4715. Puerto Rico tapped Sunrun’s home batteries for 18 straight days

Sunrun has doubled participation in its Puerto Rico virtual power plant to more than 60,000 customers, and the grid is putting those home batteries to work: It tapped into them for 18 straight days in October.

A virtual power plant (VPP) connects batteries across thousands of properties and coordinates them to supply power together.

Sunrun says its VPP network in Puerto Rico now includes nearly 70,000 batteries, frequently delivering 45 megawatts (MW) for four hours at a time. It has dispatched them more than 60 times since April, including daily deployments beginning October 13 during unusually hot weather.

For Puerto Ricans, who pay some of the highest electricity prices in the US, getting reliable power for all that money remains a problem. Residential electricity averaged 26.36 cents per kilowatt-hour in August, compared with a US average of 18.16 cents, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA).

That makes the batteries already installed at homes pretty useful. The grid can pay to tap their stored energy when supplies get tight, putting existing equipment to work without waiting for a new power plant to be built.

Sunrun’s network grew from around 4,000 customers in 2024 to more than 30,000 in 2025. It says it’s the largest aggregator in Puerto Rico’s Customer Battery Energy Sharing (CBES) program.

LUMA, the island’s grid operator, calls on CBES when it expects electricity demand or reserve needs to exceed available generation. Companies such as Sunrun then manage the battery response automatically.

Homeowners get paid for sharing energy and choose how much to keep for backup. Sunrun says most share a small portion of their total battery capacity; the company earns recurring revenue for operating the network.

Across the wider CBES program, LUMA reported in July that more than 90,000 participating customers had helped provide an average of 75 MW during generation shortfalls.

Puerto Rico’s reliability problem goes well beyond hurricanes.

Customers averaged 36 hours without power in 2025, even excluding major events, according to the US EIA. That’s up 19% from 2024. Mainland US customers generally experience about two hours a year under the same measure. Major events added another 23 hours of outages on the island.

More batteries can help, but the size of the shortfall still matters. In an April regulatory filing, participating aggregators said the program couldn’t prevent every rolling blackout in 2025 because some supply gaps exceeded its roughly 50 MW of four-hour capacity. They’re looking to enroll more batteries so the program can cover larger shortfalls.

#4714. Can Creativity Make You Happier?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 11, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

The game show Family Feud pits two families against each other in a race to find the most popular answers to silly questions like “Name something you might find in a bathtub.” If you guessed “water” and 50 of the 100 people who had been surveyed had also chosen that answer, you would get those points. If you answered “arachnid,” you might get zero points. Even though many children learned the "Itsy-Bitsy Spider" song growing up, "arachnid" would probably not be one of the most-popular answers.

Creative, unconventional, divergent thinkers might be at a disadvantage on Family Feud. Yet research demonstrates that generating creative, original thought and activity can make you happier (Tan, et al. 2021).

Moderate stress, like what you might feel when taking a test, can improve our convergent thinking—the type of thinking that's required when we want to find the right answer to a question or a problem. However, stress can stifle divergent, out-of-the-box, creative problem-solving. Divergent thinking involves generating multiple novel ideas from multiple perspectives and/or combinations of perspectives (Guo et al., 2024). When we feel looser, freer, and more relaxed, we can access our creative mind more readily.

Creativity can lower stress by offering outlets for strong emotions. Poets, authors, songwriters, dancers, and other artists find that strong emotions can fuel creativity as they strive to transform pain into beauty. Psychotherapists often recommend creative writing, journaling, and other artistic outlets as a therapeutic intervention. Creativity can increase well-being, providing opportunities to feel more fully alive and joyful (Tan, et al. 2021).

Every month, a group of friends gathers at our home for a musical jam session. We improvise songs, switch instruments, and often end by drumming on percussion instruments. This shared creativity strengthens our friendship and our sense of playfulness. Engaging in creative arts with others reduces loneliness and supports social connection, an essential requirement for happiness (Perkins, et al. 2021).

Many young people have formed deep friendships from Dungeons and Dragons, Magic: The Gathering, and similar role-playing games that require creative imagination, divergent thinking, and sometimes even elaborate costume creations.

Studies show that group-based arts and creativity programs can improve the health, well-being, and quality of life of older people. These activities strengthen social ties, encourage an active imagination, and promote physical activity, all essential for a healthy life (Sowerby, et al. 2026).

When I suggest to clients that they might improve their happiness by finding a creative outlet, I often hear, “But I’m not a creative person.” I usually ask them a few questions like, “Have you ever substituted a different ingredient in a recipe when you didn’t have the right ingredients? Or have you ever had to try different ways to teach your child how to tie shoelaces?” Typically, people can think of several times in the recent past when they have been creative.

Author, psychotherapist, and writing coach Marni Freedman writes in her delightful new book, Artistic Badassery, “The latest research on creativity from both a psychological and a neuroscientific perspective shows that creativity is not an inborn gift or a fixed trait, but rather a set of skills that can be developed through practice, effort, and the right conditions.”

Like any mental muscle, creativity needs exercise to develop. If you’re just learning to play guitar, you may not yet have enough musical vocabulary to improvise. Yet you can write a song after learning only three chords. All you need is an idea and a melody. It can be fun to create something original, even if it wouldn’t pass critical muster. Try making something just for the fun of it, without criticizing the outcome. Let yourself play in the sandbox of creativity. It might make you happier.

I think there should be a Family Feud game for divergent thinkers. You would try to pick the most novel answers to the questions asked, and the person who picks logical items that no one else chooses wins. Here’s a fun question to start: “What items might be found in a national ballroom?”

Freedman, M. 2026. Artistic Badassery: How to Unblock and Become a Creative Force of Nature. Hay House LLC.

Sowerby EJ, Doherty A, Harrison J. Arts and creativity and its impact on older people's health and wellbeing: commentary on a systematic review. Pract Nurs. 2025 Mar 2;36(3):98-103. doi: 10.12968/pnur.2024.0032. PMID: 41503028; PMCID: PMC7618590.

Tan CY, Chuah CQ, Lee ST, Tan CS. Being Creative Makes You Happier: The Positive Effect of Creativity on Subjective Well-Being. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2021 Jul 6;18(14):7244. doi: 10.3390/ijerph18147244. PMID: 34299693; PMCID: PMC8305859.

#4713. ‘2001: A Space Odyssey’ movie prop may sell for over $1 million

Published Nov 3, 2026 12:00 PM EST

Now is your chance to own as many pieces of film history as your bank account will allow. Numerous items from filmmaker Stanley Kubrick’s personal archive are hitting the auction block for the first time. Equipment, props, scripts, and more will go up for bid directly from the Stanley Kubrick Film Archives at Bonhams in London this February.

Stanley Kubrick (1928-1999) was one of Hollywood’s most respected and influential filmmakers. His most impactful films include 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968), A Clockwork Orange (1971), The Shining (1980), and Eyes Wide Shut (1999). His films pushed boundaries and left a lasting impression that extended far beyond the screen.

“His movies have stood the test of time and will continue to be relevant to our shared humanity as long as people love the art of great cinema,” Katharina Kubrick, an actor and Kubrick’s daughter, said in a statement. “We are proud to be able to share with you some of the items from this unique collection, which we hope will find new homes and be cherished until it is time to pass them on to the next generation of film lovers.”

The folding dark wood director’s chair accompanied Kubrick throughout his career. It has a pale green canvas seat and back, and each of the arms has a customised script box attached to it and the name “Stanley Kubrick” stencilled in black. It is estimated to sell for $11,000 to $16,000.

The ghostly Grady sisters Danny are amongst the most scary elements in Kubrick’s 1980 film film The Shining. Costume designer Milena Canonero said Kubrick wanted the girls to wear matching outfits that wouldn’t tie them to a specific period. Canonero took inspiration from clothing store catalogues and said she had a “1940s American style” in mind for the Grady sisters. These are expected to sell for $54,000 to $80,000

2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) is widely regarded as Kubrick’s masterpiece. The Star Child has a brief appearance at the conclusion of the film, but is highly significant. This fiberglass baby became a memorable image from the film that won the Academy Award for Best Special Effects in 1969. This lot is expected to sell for $800,000 to $1,100,000.

Kubrick had a well-documented passion for chess, and he often applied lessons he learned from the game’s discipline into his filmmaking. He developed his love for the game during his teens in New York City’s Washington Square Park, playing for hours against other chess enthusiasts and local hustlers. This chess set is estimated to sell for $2,700 to $5,400.

“Few people have had as much of an overwhelming impact on visual culture as Stanley Kubrick,” added Claire Tole-Moir, Head of Popular Culture at Bonhams. “His films provide such a striking assortment of distinctive images, that you never forget your first time watching them. His precise, bold style and technical mastery is so distinctive that the word ‘Kubrickian’ even entered the English dictionary.”

All of the items up for auction can be viewed at Bonhams website. They can also be seen in person at Bonhams Los Angeles (November 2 to November 6) and Bonhams Paris (November 16, 17, 21, 23, and 24). The live auction will take place at Bonhams in London on Wednesday,  February 3, 2027, with an online auction ending on February 4 at 12 p.m. local time.

#4711. Xiaomi’s humanoid robots work a full 8-hour shift in its EV factory

Xiaomi has released footage of its humanoid robots working a full 8-hour shift at its EV factory, sorting center console side covers for its cars. The company says the robots did it on their own, catching and fixing their own mistakes along the way.

If that’s fully autonomous, it’s truly impressive. But we’ve been disappointed by humanoid robot demos before, and Xiaomi left out the numbers that would let anyone check.

Xiaomi Tech posted the video on X on November 3, as the company picked up awards at the World Internet Conference in Wuzhen. It shows the robots pulling side covers from bins, carrying them to storage racks, and placing them into slots, with a running clock of cumulative working time and an “Autonomous, 100x Speed” label in the corner.

8 hours on the production line. 🤖Xiaomi’s full-size humanoid robot takes on an 8-hour task at the Center Console Side-Cover Sorting Workstation at Xiaomi Auto Factory.Beyond sustained operation, it can autonomously detect and correct anomalies while coordinating with the… pic.twitter.com/brpO3S5bCn

According to Xiaomi, the robot covered the full day of production needs at that workstation. The company says it detected and corrected anomalies on its own and coordinated with the production line’s control system, calling it “another step toward real-world industrial deployment.”

This is the third milestone in a program Xiaomi has been running in public all year. In March, it put a humanoid in its Beijing EV factory as an “intern” installing self-tapping nuts. Xiaomi reported a 90.2% success rate over three hours, fast enough to meet the station’s 76-second cycle time. By July, it said that success rate was up to 98%, and it added two harder stations, including the side-cover sorting job from this week’s video.

Last December, Xiaomi’s CEO, Lei Jun, said the company plans to deploy humanoid robots in large numbers across its factories within five years.

Xiaomi also announced that its open-source Xiaomi-Robotics-1 AI model, pre-trained on 100,000 hours of real-world robot data, has started trial runs in Xiaomi staff apartments. In a 30-minute run, it completed more than 50 task chains across three rooms.

Xiaomi didn’t say how many parts the robots sorted, what the success rate was over eight hours, or how many times a human had to step in. It also didn’t explain how the robots stayed powered for a full shift: swapped batteries, a tether, or charging breaks.

And that matters, because “autonomous” in a robot video can mean anything. Tesla’s Optimus robots at the 2024 “We, Robot” event were remotely operated by humans, which Tesla didn’t disclose at the time. Last December, an Optimus took a suspicious tumble in a Miami demo, raising its hands to its head like a teleoperator pulling off a VR headset as it fell.

To be fair to Xiaomi, it has published success rates and cycle times for its earlier factory tests. That’s more than Tesla has ever shared about Optimus doing useful work, and Tesla now says it won’t deliver Optimus to outside customers until late 2027.

The most interesting moment in the video comes around the 1:37 mark. In a segment Xiaomi labels “Dropped Material: Multi-Robot Collaboration,” a humanoid upper body mounted on a wheeled base rolls in to help the two legged robots.

It’s not the only thing on wheels in that scene, either. The bins of parts are shuttled around by autonomous mobile robots, the same kind of wheeled platforms that have been moving materials in car factories for years.

They could have got a lot more done if they'd moved the parts bins closer so the bots didn't have to walk as far. That's a huge open space between the two.

If this demo was truly fully autonomous for eight hours, with the robots handling their own errors, that’s one of the more impressive humanoid demos we’ve seen. Xiaomi deserves credit for putting its robots on a real production line and publishing some real numbers along the way. But we’ve been burned by “autonomous” robot demos before, so we’ll wait for more details before getting too excited.

The wheeled robot is our favorite part of the video, though. It’s a great example of why you shouldn’t bet everything on the humanoid form factor. Wheels are far more efficient than legs on most terrain, and a flat factory floor is the best-case scenario for wheels. A wheeled base doesn’t burn energy just to stay upright, it’s more stable when carrying parts, it has room for a much bigger battery (which would solve that 8-hour power question), and it needs fewer expensive actuators.

The value in these robots is in the hands, arms, and the AI driving them. Legs make sense in homes with stairs, and maybe that’s where Xiaomi wants to take them eventually. But factories were designed around carts and forklifts, not people walking around carrying parts.

#4710. Oldest recordings of Louisiana Creole discovered in Indiana archive

Published Nov 3, 2026 2:20 PM EST

A trailblazing Black linguist’s historical audio recordings have been rediscovered more than 90 years after his vital fieldwork. Originally etched onto aluminum discs, Lorenzo Dow Turner’s recordings are now the oldest known audio clips of authentic Louisiana Creole. Although the language has all-but-disappeared from daily life, the invaluable work resurfaces at a time when researchers and Creole descendents are striving to preserve—and even revive—the unique dialect.

As a language, Louisiana Creole is a distinctly American creation. Born from the international slave trade during the 18th century, the hybrid language primarily blended the French spoken by colonists and slavers with multiple West African dialects, particularly from the Senegambian region. Creole continued to evolve over ensuing generations among both enslaved and free communities, who infused French vocabulary with regionally unique grammar, sentence structures, and phrases.

“Africans with little common language were forced onto plantations where French was the language of administration. Everybody is learning approximations of French and then approximations of approximations,” Oliver Mayeux, a linguist at the University of Cambridge, recently explained. “Quite quickly, a new language is born.”

By the 19th century, Louisiana Creole was the common tongue of enslaved plantation workers and their overseers. It was also spoken by Haitian refugees, Caribbean immigrants, recently arrived Acadians from Canada, and much of New Orleans’ dock workers. Only a few thousand native Creole speakers remain today, almost all of them elderly and living in extremely rural areas of the state. But even by the 1930s, contemporary linguists like Turner understood that the language was in decline.

Although the specifics remain unclear, it appears that Turner traveled to Louisiana in 1935 to record Creole speakers for a project that ultimately never received proper funding. These clips included interviews with many people of color, including former field workers and sharecroppers. To accomplish this, Turner relied on a network of Black doctors and academics in Louisiana to find interviewees, who he then recorded in his colleagues’ private offices.

“These were trusted spaces for the participants during the era of Jim Crow segregation, and, crucially, were wired for electricity,” said Mayeux.

Recording instruments weren’t simple, portable tools at that time. Turner’s equipment consisted of a hefty microphone and two cabinet-like boxes that collectively weighed over 100 pounds.

“For these interviewees, the alien nature of the equipment alone would have made it a truly weird experience for them,” Mayeux added.

Turner apparently never published his work on Louisiana Creole, but a biography of the linguist tipped Mayeux off to the project. He eventually tracked the aluminum recording discs to Indiana University’s Archives of Traditional Music, where preservationists had already digitized them.

Mayeux was astonished to listen to the long-forgotten, clear recordings of native Creole speakers discussing their daily lives and personal histories. Some may have been more embellished than others, however. One participant, Odelia Edmond, vividly describes a childhood memory of swindling 30 cents from Zozo Labrique, a New Orleans folk figure who sold red brick dust used in protective Voodou rituals. After reviewing the clips, Mayeux described her as an “extraordinary character.”

“She had a husband who was murdered, after which she remarried. In the recording she says ‘I was so glad when they killed him,’” he said.

Another subject, George Doyle, worked as a cop until New Orleans segregated its police department around the turn of the 20th century. He remembers an instance of being assaulted by a white gang he described as a “band of rats,” which is corroborated in an archival newspaper article from 1893.

Turner’s once forgotten pivotal recordings are now available online for anyone to experience. The finds are not only a major development for researchers of Louisiana Creole, but for younger generations in the Kouri-Vini movement, a group working to revive the language in the 21st century.

“Young people are learning Creole to connect with the richness of their heritage, helping them discover a distinct identity in an increasingly homogenized world,” said Mayeux.

A word of caution to anyone fluent in French, however: don’t expect to have an advantage in your studies.

“Contemporary French speakers would simply not be able to comprehend this language,” warned Mayeux.

#4709. How Non-Dairy Creamers Doubled Coffee’s Calories For Many Americans

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Coffee consumption among U.S. adults remained relatively stable between 2003 and 2018, but the average number of calories consumed from coffee beverages increased by nearly 40%, according to a study published in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics.

By 2017–2018, U.S. adults consumed an average of about 13 ounces of coffee beverages per day. Meanwhile, the average daily calorie intake from these beverages had increased from 43 to 60 calories since 2003–2004.

By 2018, non-dairy creamer had become the largest source of calories added to coffee, surpassing sugar or syrup and dairy milk.

The researchers analyzed data from eight consecutive cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) from 2003 to 2018. The study included 30,459 U.S. adults ages 20 and older who provided two 24-hour dietary recalls.

The researchers categorized coffee beverages based on whether they contained added ingredients. These additions included:

The researchers found that coffee intake remained stable, while the average calorie intake from coffee beverages increased.

The absolute increase in caloric intake is about 17 kcal per day, which is only about 1% of a 2,000 kcal diet.

Coffee consumption was also higher among men, non-Hispanic white adults, and people with higher incomes. Those who slept fewer hours or worked longer hours also tended to drink more coffee.

In 2018, the most common coffee additions by weight were:

The researchers found no significant changes in the amounts of dairy milk, sugar or syrup, and sugar substitutes added to coffee between 2003 and 2018.

However, consumption of non-dairy additions increased during this period. Non-dairy creamer consumption rose from 3.37 to 8.08 grams per day, while non-dairy milk increased from 0.27 to 2.45 grams per day.

By 2017–2018, non-dairy creamer contributed the most calories among coffee additions:

In 2003–2004, non-dairy creamer contributed an average of 7.7 calories per day, meaning its calorie contribution more than doubled by 2017–2018.

Kristin Kirkpatrick, president of KAK, Consulting, LLC, and a dietitian at the Cleveland Clinic Department of Wellness & Preventive Medicine in Cleveland, Ohio, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings didn’t surprise her.

“The variety of coffee drinks, both at coffee houses and grocery stores, as well as options for creamers in the grocery store, make it easy to trade in black coffee for something closer to dessert,” she said.

She also added, however, that not all non-dairy creamers are created equal.

“Some are quite natural, with minimal ingredients, including no added sugars and no additives. Others are ingredient-heavy with either a large amount of sugar (real or artificial) and additives, so it’s really based on the type that is purchased,” she noted.

More than 60% of Americans drink coffee daily. Research suggests that drinking coffee with little to no added sugar or saturated fat may offer health benefits.

Previous research has associated moderate coffee consumption, typically around 3–5 cups per day, with a lower risk of several health conditions, including:

“These benefits make sense. After all, coffee beans are indeed a deeply hued plant, with multiple bioactive compounds that may strengthen health,” said Kirkpatrick.

She also cautioned consumers to be mindful of any caffeine sensitivities they may have. However, the benefits of coffee have been seen in studies assessing both caffeinated and decaf options.

However, adding ingredients high in sugar or saturated fat could offset some of coffee’s potential health benefits.

Kirkpatrick noted that some studies suggest milk may enhance antioxidant activity. The current study did not examine whether coffee additions reduced its health benefits, but found that these ingredients contributed additional calories.

Other research has raised concerns about the potential health effects of consuming excessive added sugar and certain food additives.

“I suggest that my patients try to embrace a black cup of coffee as opposed to starting the day with sugar,” Kirkpatrick said.

She suggested that certain additions, such as chicory root or cinnamon, may enhance your brew while still providing benefits. Plain milk can also provide protein and calcium without added sugar.

“Starting the day with [something] sweet may make it difficult to limit sugary foods later in the day. Starting the day with a more bitter approach may [be] an important factor in keeping sugar down, as bitter compounds may positively impact appetite-regulating pathways,” said Kirkpatrick.

BYD’s new full-size electric SUV, the Denza N9 EV, was revealed in a regulatory filing, weighing in at over 8,200 lbs (3,760 kg). That creates one issue.

The Denza N9 first went on sale last March, a flagship plug-in hybrid (PHEV) SUV with a combined CLTC range of about 807 miles (1,300 km) on a full charge and full tank of gas.

BYD introduced the updated Flash Charging version earlier this year, which uses its second-generation Blade Batteries and delivers a pure electric CLTC range of 260 miles (420 km). Combined, it gets up to 944 miles (1,520 km) under CLTC conditions.

In the latest batch of new energy vehicles (NEVs) approved for sale by China’s MIIT (Ministry of Information Technology) this week, a new all-electric Denza N9 appeared.

The filing revealed the Denza N9 EV will be available with three electric motors, delivering a combined output of 1,193 horsepower (890 kW).

A badge on the back reveals it will use BYD’s tri-motor e3 platform. The setup features a single 362 horsepower (270 kW) front motor and two 415 horsepower (310 kW) rear electric motors.

The electric version measures 5,270 mm long, 2,030 mm wide, and 1,830 mm tall, with a 3,125 mm wheelbase, which is the same as the current Denza N9 PHEV Flash Charging model. It will be available in five- and six-seat configurations.

While the filing reveals it will use a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery with cells from BYD’s battery unit, FinDreams, it does not provide specifics like capacity or driving range.

One relatively big thing to note: the Denza N9 EV has a gross weight of 3,760 kg, or about 8,289 lbs.

Obscene weight , and that applies to other SUVs as well. Vehicle registration taxes should be based on vehicle weight as it wears out roads and endangers other road users and infrastructure and wastes resources.

As AutoNext points out, this makes it too heavy for an EU category B driving license, which covers up to 3,500 kg (7,716 lbs).

Last year, the EU updated the rules, allowing drivers who have held a category B license for two years to drive alternative-fuelled vehicles with a maximum weight of up to 4,250 kg (9,369 lbs).

While the Denza N9 EV would qualify as listed, newer drivers would still need a commercial EU category C1 driving license to drive it.

BYD launched its luxury sub-brand, Denza, in Europe and the UK in March, starting with the Z9 GT and the D9 van. More recently, it introduced the Bao 5 PHEV SUV and the Denza Z electric supercar.

#4707. Innovators at Work: The Price for Breaking the Rules

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 11, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

Ethical disruptive innovators identify and solve problems through prosocial and creative means that often unsettle group norms.

Disruption can be interpreted both as destructive and divine, depending on the professional culture. For example, part-time Sherwin-Williams employee Tony Piloseno, a senior at the time at Ohio University, used his popular TikTok channel to share his paint-mixing acumen, a clever contribution meant to bolster the company’s products, yet instead of accolades, he was served termination papers for violating company policy. However, instead of accepting one of the multiple job offers spurred by the news coverage, he poured his energy into starting his own paint company, a bold innovator’s move (Tonester Paints, n.d.).

Organizational norms govern how employees typically behave at work, but norms can be messy business, for institutions possess multiple forms. There are injunctive norms, which are the “ought to” behaviors, and descriptive norms, which detail what people actually do. When a gap exists between the two, the Focus Theory of Normative Conduct suggests we follow the norms we see others live out (Cialdini et al., 1991).

For example, let’s say that during faculty meetings, university administrators regularly profess that they value employee well-being (injunctive norms), yet faculty workload dictates 70-hour work weeks, and the university gym is free to students, but not to employees. Faculty will work longer hours and exercise fewer hours, putting their health at risk, because the descriptive norm is what plays out on campus despite injunctive norms to the contrary (Cialdini et al., 1990; Roswag et al., 2026; Skogstad et al., 2017).

We are shaped by those with whom we share our social spaces, so what happens when an employee decides to think past tradition, explore new ideas, and forge unique connections in a quest to innovate novel solutions to organizational problems (Lawande, 2023)?

Dyer and colleagues (2011) studied just that, interviewing creators of groundbreaking products and founders and leaders of visionary companies. They shared their insights in the book The Innovator’s DNA: Mastering the Five Skills of Disruptive Innovators. Across their interviews, surveys, and research, five characteristics bubbled up from their data, finding that innovators passionately practice:

Another intriguing finding was that, though many companies’ leaders facilitated processes that encouraged innovation, they themselves did not engage in innovative work. Conversely, in highly innovative organizations, making up just 15 percent of Dyer et al.’s (2009) research, top executives were among the ones actually doing, not delegating, innovation. Therefore, the injunctive (ought to) and descriptive (actually doing) organizational norms were in alignment, thus providing a clear pathway for others to join in or initiate creative work.

Again, we tend to emulate what we see, and leaders set that agenda. But what happens to innovative employees in organizations where leadership views their innovator’s DNA as a threat, not an asset?

Ethical disruption awakens innovation, but as Tony experienced, shaking trees has its costs; keepers of the status quo sometimes go to considerable lengths to neutralize norm-breakers. Norm violations are categorized as either constructive, such as crafting innovative products that surpass current offerings, or destructive, like purposefully denigrating a colleague’s reputation. The disruptor’s intentions and the innovation’s success also factor into how the norm is classified (Bennett et al., 2024). Though organizations often profess a desire for “out-of-the-box” thinkers, many nonconformists face roadblocks and repercussions. Whether the disruptor receives praise or pushback is, in large part, reflective of leadership.

According to McGregor’s (1960) seminal book, The Human Side of Enterprise, leaders adopt one of two theories when developing their style of management. Leaders with a Theory X view of management assume employees are lazy and shirk responsibility; therefore, they must be micromanaged, leaving little room for innovation. In contrast, leaders who view management through a Theory Y framework believe work can be fun, employees are internally motivated to do a good job, and that when given autonomy and resources, they can and will engage in creative work. Thus, under Theory Y leadership, innovators innovate.

Another way to think about leadership approaches that stymie innovation is through what researchers call control appraisal. Leaders with a low control appraisal struggle with self-doubt and believe they have limited ability to control outcomes. This group is unsettled by innovators, viewing them as unpredictable and destabilizing. Thus, they are quick to shut them down, often using withdrawal of opportunities and ostracization as containment strategies. By contrast, leaders with high control appraisal are self-confident and possess a strong sense of personal agency, or trust that they have the skills and fortitude to impact outcomes. These leaders are intrigued by innovators and work to form genuine connections, believing disruptors’ creativity is an asset, thus supporting and celebrating their work (Peng et al., 2026).

Social comparison theory is another helpful tool for considering leaders’ level of support for ethical disruptive innovators. It posits that leaders with a low core self-evaluation, or a propensity to question their ability to steer the ship, often become jealous of employees who exhibit high leadership potential (HLP), worried their star might surpass their own, and thus attempt to eliminate the competition by withdrawing opportunities. Conversely, comparison is minimal to nonexistent in leaders with a high core self-evaluation, and this positioning calls them to support innovative projects and proposals with the potential to bolster the institution’s success and more effectively serve communities (Yu et al., 2025).

Lastly, when faced with ethically disruptive innovators who don’t conform to the prevailing work culture, knowingly or unknowingly breaking group norms, leaders tend to react in one of five ways: forgive, reward, punish, ignore, or manipulate. According to research, however, only the reward reaction ensures the creative continues to engage in innovative behaviors. So, when a leader shuts down an innovator, the employee and the organization both lose out (Lin et al., 2016).

So, what does this all tell us about the types of leaders innovators need to engage in trailblazing work? First, innovators need leaders who clearly articulate and live into their mission, ensuring their injunctive norms (ought tos) and descriptive norms (what people actually do) are in alignment. Second, innovators benefit from leaders who build authentic relationships with their employees, not just rule-followers in their inner circle. Third, innovators thrive when working for leaders who personally engage in innovative work, and by that example, the institution develops a collective culture of creativity and care.

#4705. WWII submarine returns to Michigan after extensive restoration

Published Nov 3, 2026 4:00 PM EST

A piece of World War II naval history has officially returned home to Muskegon, Michigan, looking like a brand new ship. On October 31, the USS Silversides arrived back at its museum after a 15-hour journey across Lake Michigan. The submarine was in Wisconsin for three months for its dry dock preservation in over 50 years. The endeavor involved completely removing the nearly 312-foot-long Gato-class submarine from the water in order to inspect and repair its lower hull.

Although workers noted the highly decorated vessel was holding up much better than anticipated, vessel curator Scott Hardin explained that the USS Silversides still required a sizable amount of attention. The $3.5 million repairs included welding a reinforcement steel to its underside, as well as multiple other fixes across all portions of the ship.

“Literally, from top to bottom, she got refurbished,” he told Michigan Live in a recent interview.

Built within one year and launched on August 21, 1941, the USS Silversides patrolled the Pacific theater armed with 10 torpedo tubes, a .50 caliber deck gun, as well as 40 mm and 20 mm cannons. It completed over 90,000 long tons of shipping and sank 23 enemy ships during that time. The U.S. Navy decommissioned the Silversides in 1946, and it later served as a Naval Reservist training ship in Chicago. It was later transferred to the Great Lakes Naval Memorial & Museum in 1987, before receiving its own USS Silversides Submarine Museum in Muskegon, Michigan.

“World War II vets in general are few and far between. And so what we have left from that generation are some of the machines that these guys used,” Hardin added. “It served the entire length of World War II. A man died on board, and it’s a piece of American history.”

During its dry docking earlier this year, workers also discovered another bit of unexpected U.S. history aboard the Silversides. Amid inspections, an attendant noticed a flood valve stamped with “Trigger” next to an accompanying serial number. A further review revealed the ship part is the only surviving piece of the USS Trigger, a nearly identical Gato-class submarine that sank during WWII. The Silversides and Trigger were constructed next to one another at California’s Mare Island Navy Yard, and many of their components were interchangeable with one another.

The USS Silversides is now receiving an interior cleaning before once again opening to public visitors on Saturday, November 7. However, there is still that $3.5 million repair bill to tackle. Hardin and his colleagues encourage supporters to help fund the ongoing preservation work through donating directly to the museum online.

#4704. Leading Medical Groups Team Up to Redefine Female Heart Health

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A quartet of medical organizations has published a comprehensive set of reports calling for a coordinated plan of action to improve heart healthcare for women throughout their lifetimes.

The reports detail how cardiovascular health issues can be prevented, monitored, and treated from the early years of menstruation to peak fertility age to pregnancy to perimenopause to postmenopause stages.

The report authors call for healthcare professionals to identify heart health risks early in girls and women and to coordinate care across medical specialties.

They stress that females have specific biological factors that increase their risks of cardiovascular disease. Those components include hormonal and emotional factors.

The authors note that heart disease is the number one cause of death for females in the United States, as well as the number one cause of death during pregnancy. Yet, only 44% of females are fully aware of the dangers they face from heart disease.

The organizations issuing the reports are the American Heart Association (AHA), the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.

The groups presented their findings in a trio of reports published in the AHA’s flagship journal, Circulation on October 26.

“Women experience their healthcare across clinical specialties, but it often is fragmented or disconnected,” said Sadiya Khan, MD, the chair of the collaborative writing group for the reports and a professor of cardiovascular epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago, in a news release.

“Specifically, these reports connect the dots for clinicians, for patients, and across health domains so that care is holistic and begins in adolescence, recognizing that women’s heart health is uniquely shaped by biological transitions not experienced by men — periods, pregnancy, perimenopause, and menopause.”

Experts not involved in the reports told Healthline the updates were a long time coming.

Nicole Weinberg, MD, a cardiologist at Pacific Heart Institute’s Women’s Heart Center in Santa Monica, California, said the reports present a positive framework for women’s health.

“Women have unique cardiovascular risk factors related to pregnancy and menopause, and certain traditional risk factors, including diabetes, may increase their risk of heart disease more significantly than they do in men,” noted Nissi Suppogu, MD, a cardiologist and medical director of the Women’s Heart Center at MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California.

“Recognizing these differences is essential to identifying women at risk earlier, improving prevention strategies and ensuring they receive appropriate treatment,” she said.

“I am incredibly excited to see these new reports on women’s heart health,” added Svati Shah, MD, the president-elect of the AHA, as well as the associate dean of Translational Research and the director of Precision Genomics Collaboratory in the Duke School of Medicine in North Carolina.

“They are a call to action for increasing education, research, and coordinated clinical care for women’s heart health,” Shah said.

The organizations spelled out their recommendations in three reports.

The first report is a presidential advisory that lays out a “female-specific life course approach to the prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”

In it, the authors state that “girls and women uniquely experience fragmented care” across medical fields, including pediatrics, obstetrics, and gynecology.

The authors call for a “unified life course approach that addresses the female-specific interconnectedness of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health.”

This report breaks down the life cycle for girls and women into five stages.

“Emerging data suggest that unique biologic transitions or life stages experienced by girls and women are linked with changes in [cardiovascular disease] risk, which may be due in part to physiologic changes in sex hormones,” the authors wrote.

Weinberg said this life-stage breakdown is important, especially for risk reduction.

She said issues with menstruation during the teen years may be a harbinger of heart health problems later in life. The same is true for health issues during pregnancy, especially high blood pressure or high blood sugar levels.

“We need to be aware of these heart disease risks so we’re not caught by surprise 10 to 20 years down the road,” Weinberg said.

Suppogu agreed. “Medical professionals should emphasize that heart health is a lifelong priority and prevention should begin early. Encourage girls and women to establish healthy habits, understand their cardiovascular risk factors, and maintain regular checkups, even when they feel healthy.”

“Women’s heart health has a unique constellation of risk factors and manifestations that are shaped by biological transitions that vary across a woman’s lifetime,” said Shah.

The second report is a science advisory that recommends a comprehensive plan for women’s cardiovascular care.

In it, the authors call for a system that “integrates assessment of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across life stages.”

They propose a “national infrastructure” of centers that would coordinate clinical care, education, training, research, and community engagement around women’s heart health.

“These centers can reduce fragmentation, enhance earlier risk identification, and expand opportunities to increase representation of women in clinical research,” the authors wrote. “In doing so, they offer a bold opportunity for a scalable and equitable model to improve cardiovascular health for all women.”

To illustrate their point, the authors noted that only about 60% of women with hypertensive disorders during pregnancy in the United States have a follow-up visit with a healthcare professional about their condition within the first 6 months after giving birth.

“Given that pregnancy is a cardiovascular stress test and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are risk-enhancing factors for long-term [cardiovascular disease] risk, this represents a major missed opportunity to address cardiovascular risk,” the authors wrote.

“Pregnancy and the postpartum period are important windows into cardiovascular health throughout the life course,” said William Grobman, MD, the vice-chair of the writing group for these reports and a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at The Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, in the press release.

“An adverse pregnancy outcome can unmask increased cardiovascular risk, and that information should guide care well beyond pregnancy,” he continued.

The third report is a scientific statement that suggests a “consensus guideline for the female-specific prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”

In it, the authors state that there is “growing recognition that the optimal prevention and management of cardiovascular disease in girls and women requires attention to sex-specific considerations relevant to the interconnected domains of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across the life course.”

The authors note several age-related warning signs of heart issues. These are spelled out in the AHA press release.

Females comprise around half the population, and their cardiovascular health “must be a part of everyday care across medicine,” said Mariell Jessup, MD, the chief science and medical officer of the American Heart Association, in the press release. “These publications give clinicians and health systems a shared foundation for recognizing risk throughout a woman’s life.”

In a scientific statement published in February 2026, the AHA projected that 60% of females in the United States will have at least one type of cardiovascular disease by 2050.

The organization also predicted that 25% of U.S. women will have diabetes and 60% will have obesity by that year if current trends continue.

The authors of that report listed several steps they said could reverse these trends. Among them:

Experts say women can also take action on their own to reduce their risks. Suppogu suggests the following:

These recommendations can also be found in the AHA’s Life’s Essential 8 tips for a healthy heart.

“Most importantly, we need to educate women that heart disease is not inevitable, and early intervention can help prevent it and improve long-term health,” Suppogu said.

Weinberg advised women to include plenty of fruits and vegetables and a minimal amount of meat in their daily diet. She said that women should have regular check-ups with their doctor, and that adopting a healthy lifestyle doesn’t have to be complicated.

Khan said women’s health is a community effort. “All girls and women deserve more healthy years to live their fullest lives,” she said in the press release.

“Advancing women’s health is a responsibility we all share. This investment improves not only women’s health but also the health of their families and their communities.”

#4703. Germany’s EV share hits record 37% as BEVs beat gas and diesel combined

Battery-electric cars took a record 37% of Germany’s new car market in October, according to data released today by the Kraftfahrt-Bundesamt (KBA), the country’s federal motor vehicle authority. That’s 94,086 BEVs, up 79.5% from 52,425 a year earlier.

For the second month in a row, German buyers registered more fully electric cars than gasoline and diesel cars combined. And with two months left in the year, Germany has already blown past the auto industry’s EV forecast for all of 2026.

The overall market barely grew in October. Total new car registrations rose 1.7% to 254,492 units, which means the EV growth came straight out of combustion cars.

Gasoline car registrations crashed 40.5% to 38,516 units, a 15.1% share. Diesel fell 21.6% to 23,882 units, or 9.4% of the market. Add them up and pure combustion cars made up just 24.5% of new registrations, 12.5 points less than BEVs alone.

Plug-in hybrids slipped 7.9% to 28,499 units (11.2%). So plug-ins accounted for about 48% of the German market last month, and the average CO2 emissions of new cars dropped 21.1% year-over-year to 79.4 g/km.

As we reported this summer, BEVs became the most popular powertrain in Germany for the first time in June with a 28.4% share. They’ve kept climbing every month since: 32.4% in August, 34.5% in September, and now 37% in October.

Through the first ten months of the year, Germany has registered 698,230 BEVs, up 60.7% year-over-year. That’s about 28.2% of the 2,476,290 new cars registered in 2026 so far, up from roughly 19% for the full year 2025.

And the industry didn’t see it coming. In December, the VDA, Germany’s auto industry association, forecast about 693,000 BEV registrations for all of 2026. Germany passed that in October. At the current pace, it’s on track for somewhere around 875,000 by the end of the year.

The biggest driver is Germany’s new EV incentive, which applies retroactively to cars registered since January 1. It pays €3,000 for a new BEV, bought or leased, and up to €6,000 for lower-income households with children. Households with taxable income above €80,000 (€90,000 with kids) don’t qualify.

The program targets private buyers, and that’s exactly where the KBA data shows the jump. Private registrations rose 20.6% in October, while commercial registrations fell 8.2%. Private buyers now make up 40.7% of the market.

Germany has been here before. The government killed its previous EV incentive overnight in December 2023, and BEV sales fell off a cliff in 2024. This time, the money is going to the buyers who need it most, and it’s moving the needle fast.

Tesla’s German numbers swing wildly with its quarterly delivery cycle. In September, the end of the quarter, it registered 12,552 cars (+268.7%) and the Model Y was the best-selling car in Germany. In October, it registered only 2,932, which is still up 290.9% but from a tiny base, for a 1.2% market share.

Year-to-date, Tesla is up 206.1% to 47,742 registrations. That’s a big rebound from a terrible 2025, but BYD is now slightly ahead with 47,961 (+216.1%). BYD registered 5,173 cars in October (+54.3%), though the majority of its German sales are plug-in hybrids, not BEVs.

The other Chinese brands are growing even faster. Leapmotor registered 3,661 cars in October, up 288.6%, and is at 19,705 for the year. Xpeng was up 284.4% to 1,380 units, and SAIC’s MG was up 48.5% to 4,140.

Volkswagen Group still owns the top of the EV charts, though. Through September, the Skoda Elroq was Germany’s best-selling EV with 30,845 units, ahead of the Tesla Model Y (29,464) and the VW ID.3 (24,352).

The EV boom is happening during one of the worst years in the history of Germany’s auto industry.

In October, the VW brand’s German registrations fell 4%, Audi dropped 8.4%, Porsche lost 5.7%, and Opel crashed 24.1%. BMW was flat (+0.1%), and Mercedes was the exception, up 8.5%. VW is still by far the biggest brand in Germany with an 18.2% share, but it’s down 5.6% for the year.

Last week, Volkswagen Group reported a €5.9 billion operating loss for the third quarter, its biggest quarterly loss since Dieselgate, driven by a writedown of its Porsche stake, weak sales in China, and thin EV margins. The group has already approved a plan to cut 100,000 jobs and close several German plants. Mercedes cut its 2026 car margin guidance to 2-3% last week, mainly because of China.

It’s not a product problem. VW’s new ID. Polo is sold out with over 30,000 orders, BMW has over 50,000 orders for the Neue Klasse iX3, and the Elroq leads the German EV market.

Germany is proving what we’ve been saying for years. Give buyers EVs they can actually afford, and they switch fast. Fully electric cars went from about 19% of the market last year to 37% in October, and the country beat the industry’s full-year forecast with two months to spare. That’s not a slow transition.

One thing to consider when talking about EVs not being Germany-made is that Germany car makers can't make them fast enough. A lot of the models are sold out for months. It's not an excuse but something to keep in mind.

Compare that with North America, where EV sales dropped 44% after the US killed its federal EV tax credit. Same technology, sometimes the same cars. The difference is policy.

Germany’s problem is who’s capturing the demand. Hint: it’s not German automakers.

But whose fault is that? You can’t spend years dragging your feet on electrification and lobby government back and forth on EV incentives and then complain when those who are all-in on EVs are able to take better advantage of the customer shift amid another oil crisis.
